Brazilian officials had earlier raised inquiries with Apple regarding gaming apps accessible to minors, and nearly three months later, Apple has been required to provide further information on the protective measures of its App Store within five business days. Details are as follows.

Apple faces pressure over regulatory and age verification issues

Last April, Brazilian officials issued notices to both Apple and Google, alleging that gaming apps on their app stores lacked age restrictions.

At the time, the National Secretariat for Digital Rights (Sedigi) and the National Consumer Secretariat (Senacon) wrote separately to the two companies, raising concerns about a "large number of apps" that offer or facilitate minors' access to gambling platforms.

Brazil recently passed a new law known as "ECA Digital," which requires app stores to restrict minors' access to gambling content. Apple subsequently launched age verification measures for apps rated 18+ in the country.

However, officials stated that preliminary investigations found multiple gambling apps appeared to lack proper age restrictions or federal authorisation, raising questions about the actual effectiveness of the relevant protective measures.

Although the full content of Apple's response lacked transparency, the relevant departments noted that Apple had addressed most of the initial questions, but still requested further information.

Below is the content released by Brazil's Ministry of Justice and Public Security (via Canaltech):

The clarifications sought include: how regulatory authorisation for apps listed in Brazil is verified; the technical criteria used to distinguish simulation-type apps from those involving real-money gambling, including situations where functionalities are hidden or altered after approval; and the mechanisms in place to prevent minors from accessing inappropriate content. Also requested was information on proactive monitoring procedures, risk prioritisation criteria, average takedown times after detection, and published timelines for implementing remediation measures — including details of a software update designed to prevent users under 18 from downloading apps classified as unsuitable for that age group.

The secretariat noted that Google's response was relatively weaker, and has requested more detailed explanations on how it verifies the identity of authorised operators, monitors apps whose licences have been suspended or expired, measures enforcement effectiveness, and prevents minors from searching for or downloading gambling apps.

Lastly, the secretariat has requested that the responses from Apple and Google be made public, but allows confidential information to be submitted separately on a restricted-access basis.
